Overview:
MITRE adversary emulation engineers present the methodology, development lifecycle, and execution strategy powering MITRE ATT&CK Evaluations. Using comic book metaphors to distinguish strict adversary emulation from flexible adversary simulation, the speakers explain how real-world Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) informs threat evaluations for enterprise defensive products. The presentation showcases an end-to-end emulation plan targeting the Latin American threat group Blind Eagle (APT-C-36) to demonstrate practical engineering workflows.

Key Topics:
- Methodological differences between adversary emulation (exact replication) and simulation (red teaming)
- Threat-informed testing and baseline configuration standards in MITRE ATT&CK Evaluations
- CTI adversary selection criteria: reporting freshness, organizational relevance, and TTP diversity
- End-to-end emulation plan development and MVP technique scoping using Blind Eagle (APT-C-36)

Technical Details:
The presentation establishes a foundational distinction between adversary emulation and adversary simulation: emulation requires strict, high-fidelity replication of an exact threat actor's observed tradecraft without operational deviation (analogous to Batgirl methodically picking a lock), whereas red teaming simulation allows broad approximations and flexible tool substitutions (analogous to Supergirl kicking down a door). MITRE ATT&CK Evaluations applies this strict emulation methodology to evaluate commercial security vendors within realistic test ranges. Crucially, vendor platforms are tested against their baseline out-of-the-box product configurations rather than tailored, tiered security suites, providing an objective benchmark that drives vendor detection and protection capabilities forward.

Developing an evaluation requires close synchronization between Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) analysts and red team software engineers. The adversary selection process evaluates four essential criteria: the availability of sufficient, recent open-source CTI reporting (within the past two years); direct relevance of the threat actor and their Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) to enterprise defenders; sufficient variety and depth in historical operations to support robust execution paths and operational contingencies; and distinctive technical tradecraft. While nation-state threat actors may spend years and unlimited budgets developing specialized implants, MITRE's engineering teams operate within a three-month development window, necessitating a threat-informed technique scoping process that prioritizes critical techniques into a cohesive emulation plan.

To demonstrate the execution lifecycle, the speakers presented a case study emulating the Latin American threat actor Blind Eagle (APT-C-36). Although Blind Eagle relies on more accessible, straightforward techniques rather than cutting-edge kernel exploits, their operational tradecraft represents high-priority threats that enterprise network defenders must reliably detect. The engineering team established a prioritized Minimum Viable Product (MVP) technique framework, ensuring that core malicious behaviors were successfully developed, tested in a one-week black-box evaluation, and subsequently defanged and published as open-source code for community validation and self-assessment.

Key Takeaways:
Defensive validation must be grounded in threat-informed adversary emulation that replicates exact observed attacker tradecraft rather than generic penetration testing scripts. Security leaders should evaluate detection controls against default out-of-the-box configurations to measure true baseline defensive efficacy. Red teams and threat intelligence units should collaborate closely to define Minimum Viable Product (MVP) technique scopes, enabling efficient development cycles and producing open-source, shareable emulation plans that elevate industry-wide defense.

## Overview
Presented at Black Hat USA by Yuki Osawa (Chief Engineer) and Satoru Higuchi (Senior Engineer) from the Product Security Center at Panasonic Holdings Corporation (with co-contributors Satoshi Ito, Manabu Nakano, and Takayuki Uchiyama), this session addresses IoT security from a device manufacturer's perspective. Rather than focusing solely on pre-shipment defenses, the speakers highlight the critical challenge of maintaining product security throughout post-shipment lifecycles as threat landscapes evolve.

## Post-Shipment Challenges & Evolving IoT Threat Trends
The speakers note that IoT-targeted attacks have escalated rapidly, accounting for one-third of total observed attacks in the prior year, predominantly driven by IoT malware. Key trends and operational challenges discussed include:
- **Accelerating Attack Cycles:** Malware weaponization occurs rapidly; the team observed IoT malware active in the wild just two days after a vulnerability disclosure.
- **Increasing Malware Complexity:** Threat actors are shifting away from traditional, simple IoT malware toward complex Linux-based strains. Emerging capabilities include multi-phase downloads of obfuscated modules and in-memory execution without writing files to disk.
- **Post-Shipment Security Decay:** Because device security is initially fixed at shipment, its relative effectiveness declines over time. While firmware updates are mandated by global standards, practical limits persist: end-users often fail to apply timely updates, and devices eventually hit end-of-life (EOL) when official support expires.

## The ASTIR Threat Intelligence Platform
To address post-shipment decay and support development teams, Panasonic developed an internal IoT threat intelligence project named **ASTIR** (combining *Asura*—a multi-faced, multi-armed Buddhist deity—with *TI* for Threat Intelligence).

The ASTIR architecture and workflow comprise:
- **IoT Honeypots:** Real Panasonic IoT products are deployed directly to the internet with public IP addresses. These devices are intentionally configured to be insecure to harvest attack data. Honeypots are set up in company showrooms in Japan and Taiwan.
- **Pre-Market and Custom Testing:** Operating as the device manufacturer allows the team to deploy unreleased prototypes or specially modified devices borrowed from internal business units. These units are configured with weaker defenses and expanded logging capabilities to capture granular telemetry.
- **Analysis Pipeline:** Collected samples and telemetry undergo static and dynamic analysis in dedicated IoT sandboxes. Data is mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework and VirusTotal, then synthesized using statistical visualization tools.
- **Feedback Loop:** Intelligence feeds back into pre-shipment development to establish security baselines, alert management, and educate engineering units.

## Attack Observations and Findings
Analyzing attack traffic against a subset of ASTIR honeypots using MITRE ATT&CK revealed:
- Over **99%** of observed attack actions consisted of reconnaissance and initial access.
- On devices exposing open file-sharing functions directly to the internet, attackers placed suspicious files onto the storage; however, these files were not executed and were subsequently deleted.
- Telemetry and incident reports from these observations are directly packaged and shared with internal business units to improve current and future device designs.

Overview:
Zach Wasserman and Marcos Ortiz introduce an agentless Command and Control (C2) framework that repurposes the native Windows Mobile Device Management (MDM) client stack. The speakers analyze how modern endpoint security platforms detect traditional third-party C2 agents, establishing the motivation for living-off-the-land communication channels. The presentation reveals how adversaries can establish persistent, privileged, bidirectional HTTPS control by programmatically enrolling compromised endpoints into rogue MDM servers.

Key Topics:
- Limitations of traditional agent-based C2: network anomalies, unapproved processes, and registry persistence
- Architectural criteria for native Windows living-off-the-land communication channels
- Evaluation of built-in Windows technologies: GPO, WMI, WinRM, WNS, and the MDM client stack
- Exploiting the MS-MDM and MS-MDE2 protocols for programmatic rogue server enrollment and payload delivery

Technical Details:
Traditional C2 frameworks require deploying custom agent binaries on victim endpoints. These agents inevitably generate significant detection footprints monitored by modern Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions, including anomalous outbound network connections, unapproved binary executions, and standard persistence mechanisms (such as scheduled tasks or run keys). To bypass these defensive layers, the researchers sought to identify built-in Windows client-server components capable of functioning as agentless C2 channels. They established rigorous selection criteria: client-server bidirectional control, transport-layer HTTPS encryption, extensible protocol design, persistent privileged execution surviving system reboots, and the ability to execute secondary payloads.

The speakers evaluated multiple native Windows technologies against this matrix. Group Policy Objects (GPOs) and WMI were eliminated because they operate exclusively on local networks without native HTTPS transport. Windows Remote Management (WinRM) was dismissed because its client listener is not exposed by default over external networks, and Windows Push Notification Services (WNS) proved unsuitable due to severe limitations in executing custom secondary payloads. In contrast, the native Windows MDM client—shipped system-wide since the initial release of Windows 10—satisfied all functional criteria, running as a highly privileged service and utilizing HTTPS transport.

The Windows MDM architecture comprises enrollment logic and management logic governed by open Microsoft specifications, primarily the MS-MDE2 protocol. Although Microsoft operates its commercial Intune MDM server, the underlying protocol is fully documented, enabling researchers to build custom third-party MDM servers. The MDM client exposes local APIs that allow any unprivileged application or script to initiate a programmatic enrollment. During enrollment, the client executes a sequence of SOAP-based HTTPS exchanges with the rogue server, obtaining endpoints, exchanging mutual authentication, and receiving an identity certificate alongside provisioning profiles. Once enrolled, the management service periodically checks in over HTTPS to receive and execute SyncML management commands, providing persistent, privileged execution entirely indistinguishable from legitimate enterprise management traffic.

Key Takeaways:
Adversaries can achieve stealthy, persistent, and agentless command and control by abusing legitimate administrative subsystems like the Windows MDM client. Defensive teams must expand threat hunting beyond traditional executable binaries to inspect anomalous device management enrollments and untrusted MDM server connections. Enterprise detection engineers should monitor programmatic MDM enrollment API calls and audit client certificates within the device management certificate store to uncover rogue MDM configurations.

## Overview

The presentation, delivered by a Tech Policy Fellow at UC Berkeley alongside colleague Jonathon Penney (affiliated with Osgoode and Harvard), addresses the risks surrounding AI trust and automation. The talk explores the disconnect between human trust and machine capabilities, highlighting how excessive reliance on automated systems leads to failure. To mitigate these risks, the speakers propose looking toward established frameworks in standard-setting and certification, drawing parallels to safety testing bodies like Underwriters Laboratories (UL).

## Human Behavior and Automation Bias

The talk highlights empirical research showing that humans routinely exhibit automation bias—a phenomenon studied since the 1990s—where individuals place high levels of trust in systems with minimal or inappropriate capabilities:

* **The University of Hertfordshire Companion Robot Study**:
  * Participants were invited to a home under the premise of cooking lunch with a friend.
  * A companion robot nudged participants to clear a cluttered table containing a laptop, letters, and a bottle.
  * The robot issued unusual instructions, including pouring orange juice into a potted plant and providing the password ("Sunflower") to unlock its owner's laptop.
  * Despite the robot being made intentionally inept (such as executing loops and playing classical music when asked for "robot music"), **67% of participants poured orange juice into the plant**, and **100% of the 40 participants complied with unlocking the laptop and disclosing information**.
  * When questioned, participants rationalized their actions (e.g., assuming the orange juice was "plant food" despite its smell).

* **Emergency Evacuation Study (Ayanna Howard and Team)**:
  * In a simulated building fire, every single recruited participant chose to follow a robot to safety rather than exiting through visible, bright green exit signs.
  * Participants rationalized their compliance during fight-or-flight conditions by assuming the robot must be specifically programmed for emergency guidance, despite receiving no instructions indicating that capability.

The speaker concludes that the core vulnerability is not simply trusting AI, but *over-trusting* its automation capabilities—such as trusting an usher robot to provide gardening guidance or snoop into private computers.

## The Role of Standards and Certifications

To address the risks of over-trusting automated systems, the speaker proposes establishing robust standards and independent certifications, analogous to the UL (Underwriters Laboratories) mark found on household electrical appliances:

* **Comprehensiveness**: Effective standards clearly define scope—not only stating which devices or appliances are covered (such as toasters and rotisserie ovens), but also explicitly specifying what is excluded (such as fondue pots).
* **Concreteness**: Standards define precise, objective testing procedures and criteria. For example, appliance standards specify physical drop tests and precise visual charts defining what constitutes "burnt toast" versus a "burnt waffle."
* **Constituent Testing**: Testing occurs not only at the holistic system level but drills down into individual components (e.g., thermostats, internal wiring, external panels). This enables designers to construct an approved, reliable system composed entirely of pre-certified sub-components.

Overview:
Tomer Bar and Shmuel Cohen of SafeBreach demonstrate how endpoint detection and response (EDR) agents can be weaponized into unauthenticated remote data wipers. The authors explore the architecture of static signature engines, demonstrating how remotely implanting minimal malware byte signatures into legitimate files causes security agents to automatically delete critical files. The presentation details automated black-box signature minimization against Windows Defender and the mechanics of remote, zero-privilege file destruction across operating systems.

Key Topics:
- Weaponizing endpoint security: turning EDR automatic quarantine mechanisms into remote wipers
- Prior SafeBreach research: the "Aikido" TOCTOU deletion flaw and signature update manipulation
- Black-box signature extraction and automated minimization using VirusTotal queries
- Windows Defender threat severity structures (MpThreat, MpThreatDetection) and signature optimization

Technical Details:
Building upon previous SafeBreach vulnerability research—such as Or Yair's "Aikido" attack abusing Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race conditions in EDR file deletion routines, and subsequent research manipulating Defender signature updates—the speakers investigated remote attack surfaces. Security vendors have spent decades fine-tuning static byte signature engines to minimize false positives, creating deep organizational trust in signature-driven detections. The researchers realized that if an attacker can remotely cause an EDR's static engine to misidentify a benign, critical operating system or enterprise data file as a known severe threat, the EDR will automatically delete or quarantine the file without human authorization, achieving remote data wiping without local code execution.

To discover functional minimal signatures, the team adopted a black-box approach against Windows Defender. Using VirusTotal API hunting queries, they searched for Microsoft-detected malware binaries under 200 bytes in size, retrieving 3,600 samples across families such as Joke:VBS/Terrier (120 bytes). They developed an automated minimization script that systematically trimmed characters from each sample while repeatedly saving the file to disk to verify whether Defender still detected it. Reversing Defender's scanning engine revealed internal classes MpThreat (containing the SeverityID field) and MpThreatDetection (containing an action bitmask defining mitigation steps). Only threats categorized at the highest severity level ("Severe") triggered automatic, non-interactive deletion rather than requiring manual administrator review.

The 3,600 samples yielded 130 unique signature clusters. The researchers tested candidates for real-world injection feasibility: the standard EICAR antivirus test file and its Base64 variant were rejected because EICAR specifications require the string to comprise the exact, entire file content. Ultimately, the team isolated a 15-character signature containing alphanumeric characters, a forward slash, and curly braces that reliably triggered Defender's automatic deletion engine. By remotely appending or injecting this compact byte sequence into target files—via unauthenticated network services, web caching, logging pipelines, or shared repositories—an external attacker can force the victim host's EDR to permanently destroy databases, system libraries, and critical operational documents.

Key Takeaways:
Automated EDR file remediation mechanisms present a dangerous dual-use vulnerability that adversaries can exploit for remote denial of service and data destruction. Security vendors must introduce safeguards that prevent automatic, irreversible file deletions on system-critical directories, regardless of static signature matches. System administrators and defenders should configure EDR policies to restrict automatic remediation on sensitive operational data, mandating administrative confirmation or non-destructive quarantine isolation for critical file paths.

TU Berlin researchers present a hardware-based jailbreak of modern Tesla vehicles equipped with AMD Ryzen-based infotainment and connectivity ECUs (MCU-Z / Car Computer). The authors demonstrate how physical access to the car computer enables bypassing AMD Platform Secure Boot (PSB) using voltage fault injection. By compromising the root of trust, the researchers gain persistent root access to the infotainment operating system, unlock software-gated features like rear heated seats, and extract hardware-bound cryptographic keys from the firmware TPM (fTPM).

Key Topics:
- Hardware voltage glitching and fault injection against AMD Platform Secure Boot (PSB).
- Tesla infotainment ECU architecture transitioning from Intel/Nvidia to AMD Ryzen processors.
- Bypassing dm-verity and secure boot signature checks to obtain root access.
- Arbitrary modification of Tesla Gateway configurations to enable soft-locked paid features.

Technical Details:
Tesla's modern infotainment and connectivity electronic control unit (located behind the glove box) relies on an AMD Ryzen SoC featuring an embedded AMD Secure Processor (ASP/PSP), SPI flash storage, and an NVMe drive partitioning system and user data. The boot process enforces a hardware root of trust: SPI-stored firmware and the Linux kernel are cryptographically verified through AMD PSB and dm-verity to prevent unauthorized tampering. Rather than relying on network-based browser exploits (such as historical WebKit/Chromium sandbox escapes), the researchers targeted the physical hardware using low-cost voltage glitching equipment.

By monitoring SPI traces and SVI2 power management bus communications between the CPU and the voltage regulator, the team identified the exact time window when the AMD root key verification occurs during early boot. Flipping bits in the verification process halted boot activity, confirming the critical timing window. Using an FPGA and microcontroller setup, they injected precise voltage drops on the CPU core voltage rail, corrupting the comparison logic in the AMD Secure Processor. This successful glitch allowed execution of a modified bootloader and kernel patched to ignore file system corruptions, completely bypassing signature enforcement and launching an interactive root SSH shell.

With root access secured on the infotainment OS, the researchers interacted with the internal vehicle network and modified the vehicle Gateway configuration (altering parameter ID 13 from 0 to 1), instantly enabling factory-disabled soft-locked features including the $300 rear heated seat upgrade. Furthermore, they analyzed the AMD fTPM architecture, which seals critical data including disk encryption keys for the NVMe user partition and unique Tesla vehicle authentication credentials. By reverse engineering the tree of TPM objects derived from the primary seed, they demonstrated the ability to unseal and extract hardware-bound cryptographic secrets.

Key Takeaways:
Software-gated feature locking and hardware-rooted security models are inherently vulnerable when adversaries possess physical access to vehicle hardware and buses. Automobile manufacturers must recognize that cryptographic roots of trust in consumer hardware can be circumvented via fault injection without access to private signing keys. Defending modern vehicles against physical attacks requires robust fault detection mechanisms, tamper-resistant silicon packaging, and off-vehicle cryptographic attestation that invalidates compromised vehicle identities on the backend.

talks.aiSummary:
## Overview: Defense-in-Depth and the Role of RASP

In application security and incident response, defense technologies operate across distinct layers:
- **Web Application Firewalls (WAF):** Positioned at the gateway layer, WAF inspects raw network traffic to block attacks. However, it struggles with payload variations and complex encodings processed by downstream middleware.
- **Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP):** Situated at the application layer, RASP addresses vulnerabilities by evaluating rich in-process context—including raw traffic, executed methods, and final triggered actions—allowing it to make more accurate interception decisions than WAF.
- **Host-based Intrusion Prevention Systems (HIPS):** Deployed at the host layer, HIPS activates when higher tiers fail. Its visibility is limited to process trees and basic operational metadata (e.g., unable to distinguish benign DNS traffic from data exfiltration via DNS tunneling).

Despite RASP's contextual advantages, conventional implementations implemented within high-level language runtimes remain vulnerable and suffer from inherent performance bottlenecks.

## Shortcomings and Bypass Techniques in Conventional RASP

Traditional high-level programming language (HPL) RASP implementations—often relying on bytecode instrumentation (e.g., hooking `Runtime.getRuntime().exec` in Java)—can be bypassed through three primary mechanisms:

1. **Routing / Breaking Execution Flow:** Attackers can tamper with the RASP engine's execution path using reflection or bytecode re-transformation (e.g., toggling internal boolean/key flags via reflection or leveraging `Instrumentation` to re-transform defense bytecode).
2. **Breaking Data Flow:** Attackers can defeat rule-checking logic by altering analyzer data models. Techniques include forging stack traces by spawning new threads or modifying in-memory rule sets directly using internal unsafe operations (e.g., `sun.misc.Unsafe`).
3. **Exploiting Blind Spots:** Attackers invoke targets outside the monitored scope. In Java, `Runtime.exec` ultimately invokes the native method `forkAndExec`, which calls `Java_java_lang_ProcessImpl_forkAndExec` in `libjava.so`/JVM via foreign function interfaces. Attackers can bypass bytecode hooks by invoking native methods or internal endpoints directly via reflection or foreign function interfaces (FFI).

## Stack Trace Performance Bottlenecks

A primary advantage of RASP is accessing high-level language stack traces, but conventional acquisition mechanisms introduce severe performance penalties:
- **FFI / JNI Overhead:** In JVMTI-based RASP, retrieving the Java stack trace involves calls like `Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace()`, invoking native dump functions across the FFI boundary, which is substantially slower than intra-native operations.
- **Excessive Frame Retrieval:** Standard HPL APIs dump all stack frames indiscriminately. In frameworks such as Spring Boot, an attack trace (e.g., RCE) can span hundreds or thousands of frames due to deep middleware and framework registration pipelines. However, inspection of only the top 10 frames is typically sufficient to make an interception determination.

## Proposed Direction: Low-Level RASP Architecture

To overcome the security blind spots and performance bottlenecks of traditional HPL-level defenses, the researchers propose shifting RASP into native/low-level space. Key design directions identified include:
- **Direct Native-Space Stack Unwinding:** Extracting high-level programming language stack traces directly from native space rather than making costly round-trip FFI/JNI calls.
- **Custom Frame Range Collection:** Bounding stack collection to a configurable frame range (e.g., the top 10 frames) instead of unrolling entire multi-thousand-frame call stacks, drastically cutting execution overhead while retaining necessary security context.

Overview:
This presentation examines the emerging psychological and technical threat landscapes surrounding AI assistants and autonomous "digital twins." Drawing from historical digital twin applications in nuclear power plants and autonomous vehicle driver modeling, the speaker analyzes the evolution toward Electronic Life Facilitators (ELFs) that act, write, and negotiate on behalf of humans. The talk systematically maps the multidimensional attack surfaces capable of subverting digital twins to execute adversarial objectives while impersonating the user.

Key Topics:
- Evolution of digital twins: from industrial VR simulation to autonomous AI proxies (ELFs)
- Data provenance challenges, data poisoning, and emerging "LLM SEO" manipulation
- Architecture and supply chain risks: model weights, hyperparameters, and human feedback (RLHF)
- Software stack subversion via shadow prompts, output manipulation, and adversarial suffixes

Technical Details:
The concept of a digital twin originated in high-reliability engineering, such as nuclear reactor simulations at MIT and virtual reality architectural inspections, before migrating to autonomous vehicle systems that probabilistically model human driver aggression and velocity preferences. With the emergence of foundation models, digital twin technology is transitioning to consumer software, exemplified by influencer bots like Caryn AI and automated enterprise meeting proxies known as Electronic Life Facilitators (ELFs). These autonomous agents utilize synthetic voice generation, deepfake video rendering, and behavioral language modeling to interact with third parties on behalf of a human user, introducing unprecedented trust relationships and severe attack surfaces.

The speaker deconstructs the multi-layer attack surface of digital twin systems, beginning with data provenance. Given the vast size of modern models (such as GPT-4), comprehensive data auditing is impossible, allowing adversaries to exploit data scarcity in niche domains through targeted data poisoning and "LLM SEO" manipulation. At the infrastructure layer, model weights, hyperparameter tuning, and loading configurations represent high-value insider threat surfaces, as underscored by the White House's 2023 safety commitments with leading AI labs. Furthermore, the Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipeline introduces vulnerabilities, as human annotators and overseas labeling workforces can be targeted or manipulated to embed selective behavioral biases into the model's reward functions.

At the software integration layer, the speaker highlights "shadow prompts"—mechanisms where middleware or malicious extensions silently append adversarial instructions to user queries without the user's awareness. While traditional linguistic jailbreaks like "DAN" (Do Anything Now) can be mitigated via defensive system prompting, algorithmic vulnerabilities like adversarial suffixes represent an unpatchable structural risk. By appending mathematically optimized token sequences to inputs, adversaries can reliably force the underlying model to bypass all alignment constraints, effectively co-opting the digital twin to pursue external, hostile agendas while retaining the user's identity and authority.

Key Takeaways:
As AI systems evolve from informational chatbots into autonomous digital twins with executive authority, their compromise transitions from informational leakage to direct identity usurpation. Organizations deploying AI proxies must implement cryptographic attestation, strict prompt boundaries, and provenance auditing to protect model weights and training datasets. Security architectures must monitor for shadow prompts, intercept adversarial token suffixes, and enforce human-in-the-loop verification for high-consequence decisions executed by automated proxies.

talks.title: Defender-Pretender: When Windows Defender Updates Become a Security Risk
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Defender-Pretender: When Windows Defender Updates Become a Security Risk.
talks.summary: Black Hat session on Defender-Pretender: When Windows Defender Updates Become a Security Risk.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Tomer Bar and Omer Attias, security researchers at SafeBreach, present an analysis of vulnerabilities within the Microsoft Windows Defender update mechanism. Motivated by historic state-sponsored threats like the Flame malware that hijacked Windows Update via network spoofing, the authors investigated whether a local unprivileged attacker could take over Defender's update process. The talk details the reverse engineering of Defender's signature update pipeline, reveals fundamental cryptographic verification deficiencies in Virus Definition Modules (.vdm), and demonstrates the WD-Pretender framework used to blind Defender, bypass detections, and induce permanent denial of service.

Key Topics:
- Architecture of Windows Defender signature updates: mpam-fe.exe, mpsigstub.exe, and VDM databases
- Reverse engineering the VDM format: RMDX headers, raw zlib compression, and unencrypted threat structures
- Flaws in update verification: JAMCRC checksum validation and unprotected Delta merge algorithms
- Weaponization via WD-Pretender: signature deletion, friendly file hash spoofing, and OS-wide denial of service

Technical Details:
Windows Defender distributes intelligence updates inside mpam-fe.exe (Microsoft Protection Antimalware Front-End). Upon execution, the binary extracts a CAB archive containing the core scanning engine (mpengine.dll), an updater stub (mpsigstub.exe), and four Virus Definition Module (.vdm) files split into Base and Delta pairs. The updater stub communicates with Defender's main service (MsMpEng.exe) via an RPC interface (MPsvc, function 42: ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature). Because MsMpEng operates as a Protected Process Light (PPL), replacing mpengine.dll directly fails due to digital signature enforcement. However, auditing the ingestion of .vdm files in LoadDatabase and ConsumeInputCompressed revealed that VDM files lack digital signature validation by the PPL service.

The researchers analyzed the proprietary VDM structure, finding it formatted as a PE container without executable code. Inside the resource section, data begins with an RMDX header followed by zlib-compressed blocks stripped of standard zlib magic bytes. Decompressing the Base VDM revealed over 2.5 million plaintext, unencrypted signatures categorized by threat headers (type 0x5C) and terminators (type 0x5D). While Defender inspects the compressed stream using JAMCRC (1 - CRC32) and checks expected size and CRC fields during incremental Delta merging, these mechanisms rely entirely on non-cryptographic checksums. When merging Delta actions (CopyFromDelta and CopyFromBase) to patch Base signatures in memory, Defender does not verify signature integrity against a cryptographic trust anchor.

The researchers developed WD-Pretender to weaponize these integrity flaws from an unprivileged context. First, the tool excised all signatures associated with the 'lazagne' credential recovery tool from the VDM database, allowing unprivileged execution without detection. Second, the researchers targeted Defender's 'friendly file' allowlist mechanism, which whitelists legitimate binaries (such as Oracle VirtualBox runtime libraries) via SHA-256 hashes to minimize false positives. By overwriting an Oracle hash with the SHA-256 hash of Mimikatz, Defender treated Mimikatz as an approved friendly file, allowing unhindered credential dumping. Finally, by appending the universal DOS stub string ('This program cannot be run in DOS mode') to the Emotet signature definition, Defender identified every PE binary, DLL, and driver across the operating system as Emotet malware, systematically deleting critical system files and rendering the host permanently unbootable.

Key Takeaways:
Antivirus and EDR products must enforce strict cryptographic signature validation on auxiliary definition files rather than relying solely on non-cryptographic checksums like CRC or JAMCRC. Security architectures running privileged or PPL processes must not delegate database parsing or incremental merge operations to untrusted or unauthenticated local file inputs. Organizations should monitor unexpected modifications to local definition caches, employ continuous security validation against security agents, and ensure endpoint protection agents fail closed when definition integrity is violated.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Kill Latest MPU-based Protections in Just One Shot: Targeting All Commodity RTOSes
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Kill Latest MPU-based Protections in Just One Shot: Targeting All Commodity RTOSes.
talks.summary: Black Hat session on Kill Latest MPU-based Protections in Just One Shot: Targeting All Commodity RTOSes.
talks.aiSummary:
## Overview

Real-Time Operating Systems (RTOSes) are widely deployed in safety- and mission-critical embedded domains, including aerospace, healthcare, electric vehicles, network routers, and industrial automation. To enforce memory safety and isolation, modern RTOSes increasingly rely on hardware memory protection mechanisms. Specifically, 81% of surveyed RTOSes support Memory Protection Units (MPUs), whereas only 15% support Memory Management Units (MMUs), making MPUs the predominant hardware-enforced isolation primitive in embedded systems.

The researchers analyzed six commercial MPU-based RTOSes—including **FreeRTOS**, **RT-Thread**, **Zephyr**, **ThreadX**, **SafeRTOS**, and **embOS**—investigating whether MPU-based defenses can be bypassed. Their findings show that despite MPU enforcement, architectural and design weaknesses allow attackers to achieve arbitrary read/write, privilege escalation, and information leakage.

---

## MPU Role in Mitigating Classical Exploitation

An MPU controls memory region access permissions (read, write, execute) based on the current execution state (privileged vs. unprivileged):
- **Classical Exploitation Case Study (Black Hat USA 2021):** An over-the-air (OTA) update mechanism parses files received over the network via a vulnerable parsing routine (`get_entity_file`). Controllable file size parameters combined with missing integer validation in `malloc` lead to an integer overflow, allocating an undersized heap buffer. A subsequent memory copy triggers a heap overflow.
- **Traditional Attack Target:** Attackers overwrite an HTTP request handler function pointer within an array in the heap, diverting execution to injected shellcode in read-write-execute memory.
- **MPU Mitigation:** Deploying an MPU enforces non-executable (`W^X` / NX) heap permissions. Injecting shellcode directly into data regions causes a hardware fault, neutralizing simple code injection attacks and appearing to act as a barrier against exploitation.

---

## FreeRTOS MPU Implementation & Memory Layout

The talk details FreeRTOS on the ARMv7 architecture, which uses MPU regions to enforce privilege isolation between user tasks and the kernel:
- **Region Allocation:** A total of eight MPU regions are configured, consisting of five predefined system regions and three user-defined regions.
  - **Region 7:** Kernel stack and heap (Read/Write, Non-executable in privileged state).
  - **Region 6:** Kernel code (Read-only, Executable in privileged state).
  - **Region 5:** Trampoline functions and task code (Read-only, Executable in both privileged and unprivileged states).
  - **Region 4:** Peripherals/RAM (Read/Write, Non-executable in privileged and unprivileged states).
  - **Task Stack Region:** Individual task stack (Read/Write, Non-executable in both privileged and unprivileged states).
  - **Unmapped Memory:** Any physical address not explicitly mapped defaults to Read/Write in privileged mode.
- **Task Switching & Isolation:** Unprivileged tasks (e.g., Task B) cannot access kernel code/data or other tasks' stacks. During context switches, MPU configurations are swapped; privileged tasks (e.g., Task A) retain unrestricted access.

---

## Identified Security Weaknesses

The researchers identified multiple security vulnerabilities across commercial RTOSes:
- **Missing Legacy Checks During Mode Switches:** FreeRTOS exposes wrapper functions with an `MPU_` prefix (trampoline functions). These trampolines facilitate transitioning execution from unprivileged user mode to privileged kernel mode. Unprivileged tasks invoke these trampolines, but insufficient validation during mode switching introduces exploitable flaws.
- **Cross-OS Vulnerabilities:** Across the six investigated RTOSes (FreeRTOS, RT-Thread, Zephyr, ThreadX, SafeRTOS, and embOS), systemic issues enable attackers to circumvent MPU memory boundaries, resulting in unauthorized read/write access, privilege escalation to kernel mode, and confidential memory leaks.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Evading Logging in the Cloud: Bypassing AWS CloudTrail.

talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Nick Frichette of DataDog details vulnerability research into bypassing AWS CloudTrail, the foundational audit logging service for Amazon Web Services. The presentation explores the internal serialization architectures of the AWS API across multiple service SDKs, explaining how protocol handling oversights on the AWS side of the shared responsibility model undermine security logging. Frichette demonstrates how mutating HTTP headers enables attackers to conduct completely silent IAM permission enumeration across dozens of services without generating CloudTrail events.

Key Topics:
- AWS CloudTrail architecture, threat detection role, and shared responsibility boundaries
- AWS API internals: model-first design, SDK models in Botocore, and the six AWS API protocols
- The JSON 1.1 protocol structure, x-amz-target headers, and content-type versioning
- CloudTrail evasion via protocol mutation: silent IAM permission enumeration across 645+ actions

Technical Details:
AWS CloudTrail serves as the foundational security monitoring mechanism across AWS environments, recording API invocations alongside critical metadata including caller identity, timestamp, service action, source IP, user agent, and request parameters. When adversaries compromise Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials, their primary detection risk stems from CloudTrail logs analyzed by SIEMs and data lakes. Consequently, adversaries who can execute API calls without generating CloudTrail records become entirely invisible to defensive teams. Frichette emphasizes that true CloudTrail bypasses are not customer misconfigurations or disabled trails, but underlying implementation flaws within AWS service endpoints that fall squarely under AWS's operational responsibility.

The research exploited AWS's "model-first design" architecture, where service schemas are formally defined prior to implementation. These service models, readily extractable from client SDKs like Python's Botocore library, document the six distinct communication protocols used across the AWS API ecosystem. For example, AWS Secrets Manager implements the JSON protocol version 1.1 (application/x-amz-json-1.1), requiring POST requests to the root path with an x-amz-target header specifying the target service action. The content-type header strictly dictates the serialization version used by the server to parse request bodies and route telemetry to CloudTrail.

Frichette discovered a critical protocol mutation flaw: by maliciously altering the content-type header to specify an incompatible protocol version—such as submitting an application/x-amz-json-1.0 header to a JSON 1.1 service endpoint—the AWS request handler executed authorization logic before failing protocol serialization. If the calling IAM identity possessed permission to execute the requested action, the API endpoint returned an HTTP 404 (Not Found) error; if the identity lacked permission, it returned an HTTP 403 (Access Denied). Crucially, because the mutated request failed serialization, CloudTrail completely omitted logging the transaction. This behavioral discrepancy created an undetectable oracle affecting over 645 actions across more than 40 AWS services, allowing attackers to silently brute-force their entire permission set without triggering the noisy AccessDenied alert spikes typically flagged by tools like enumerate-iam.

Key Takeaways:
Cloud providers' internal request handling and logging pipelines must be treated as complex attack surfaces that can fail silently when exposed to protocol anomalies. Cloud defenders cannot assume CloudTrail logs capture all adversarial reconnaissance, as protocol mutation vulnerabilities can suppress event generation entirely. Security teams must correlate auxiliary cloud telemetry—such as VPC flow logs and application access logs—alongside identity behavioral profiling to detect anomalous activity that bypasses control-plane logging.

## Overview and Introduction

In "How NOT to Train Your Hack Bot: Dos and Don'ts of Building Offensive GPTs," speakers Ariel (Ari) Herbert-Voss and Shane Caldwell discuss the realistic application of large language models (LLMs) to offensive security and bug bounty workflows. Herbert-Voss introduces himself as an early LLM researcher who was the first security researcher at OpenAI and contributed to GPT-3 and Codex. Caldwell is introduced as an experienced specialist in AI for offense. Both work at Run Sybil, where they build and apply models intended to automate hacker intuition.

Addressing media narratives suggesting ChatGPT either empowers low-skilled actors to execute attacks effortlessly or is entirely useless, the speakers assert that the reality lies between these extremes. Their presentation focuses on how generative Transformers function, their security-relevant limitations and capabilities, and practical offensive security use cases.

## LLM Architecture and the Lookup Table Model

Herbert-Voss contrasts Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) with classical discriminative models traditionally used in information security, such as those trained for malware classification:
* **Generative vs. Discriminative:** Unlike discriminative models that classify data, Transformers generate new text by predicting the next token in a sequence.
* **Mechanism:** Conceptually, an LLM functions as an adaptive lookup table or a compressed representation of training data.
* **Token Representation:** Words are broken down into tokens, which are integers representing parts of words.
* **Attention Mechanism:** During training, dynamic key-value pairs are created for each input token by generating key, query, and value vectors for every position in the token sequence. Attention weights are obtained by computing the similarity between these vectors. Model weights (such as Llama weights) represent this compressed data representation, which is sampled to complete input sequences.

## In-Context and Few-Shot Learning

The speakers demystify how models perform advanced reasoning or mathematical calculations from simple next-token prediction:
* **Few-Shot / In-Context Learning:** Models do not require retraining on large datasets for specific tasks. Instead, users provide a base model with a small pattern of examples directly in the input sequence.
* **Implicit Conceptual Inference:** Just as a human hacker understands that converting hexadecimal `2A` yields decimal `42` based on accumulated background knowledge without step-by-step arithmetic instructions, an LLM infers patterns and operations from semantic associations embedded across its training data.
* **Context Window and Chat Implementation:** In-context learning operates inside a defined context window where prompt text is placed. Chat interfaces implement this by loading a structured script simulating an exchange between a user and an assistant, prompting the underlying model to complete the script by mimicking observed conversational patterns.

talks.teaser: Monitoring investigates Lifting the Fog of War.

Overview:
Steve, a security researcher at Akamai with a background in Windows incident response and threat hunting, presents a defensive analysis of Microsoft Remote Procedure Call (MSRPC). Despite originating in the 1990s, MSRPC remains a ubiquitous protocol heavily leveraged by adversaries for credential theft, privilege escalation, and lateral movement in enterprise environments. The presentation examines MSRPC internal architecture and outlines defensive strategies utilizing Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) and Windows Firewall RPC filters to overcome traditional network inspection blind spots.

Key Topics:
- Adversarial exploitation of MSRPC (DCSync, PsExec, WMI, PetitPotam, ZeroLogon)
- Protocol architecture: IDL, MIDL compiler, UUIDs, bindings, and dynamic endpoints
- Limitations of network-based RPC inspection and ephemeral port tracking
- Telemetry enrichment and defense via Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) and Windows Firewall

Technical Details:
MSRPC serves as a fundamental inter-process communication backbone in Windows, underpinning key administrative and domain functions. Steve illustrates that MSRPC is prominently represented across the MITRE ATT&CK matrix, specifically highlighting DCSync for credential dumping, PsExec via the Service Control Manager and WMI for lateral movement, and critical vulnerabilities such as PetitPotam and ZeroLogon. Furthermore, threat intelligence indicates that the vast majority of modern ransomware groups maintain or actively deploy PsExec capabilities during attacks.

Defending against MSRPC attacks presents significant operational hurdles. MSRPC encapsulates application requests inside higher-level protocols running across ephemeral TCP ports or SMB named pipes, making deep packet inspection resource-intensive for network appliances. Host-level visibility is similarly challenged because RPC servers predominantly execute inside protected processes or generic svchost.exe instances. Crucially, client calls routed through the rpcrt4.dll runtime library via NdrClientCall marshal parameters without transmitting human-readable function names across the wire or API interfaces; instead, functions are identified strictly by numerical operation numbers (OpNums) defined in the server's Interface Definition Language (IDL) file compiled with the MIDL compiler.

To bridge these visibility gaps, defenders can leverage built-in Windows instrumentation. Communication begins when clients query the RPC Endpoint Mapper on well-known TCP port 135 to resolve dynamic server endpoints associated with a specific interface UUID. By tapping into native Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) providers for RPC, security teams can decode OpNums, capture interface UUIDs, and monitor client-server bindings without relying on unstable user-mode hooks or third-party process injection. Steve additionally demonstrates how native Windows Firewall RPC filters can restrict unauthorized RPC communications to sensitive endpoints.

Key Takeaways:
Security operations teams cannot rely exclusively on standard network metadata or ephemeral port monitoring to detect MSRPC-based lateral movement and privilege escalation. Organizations should deploy host-level ETW logging to capture interface UUIDs and resolve OpNums to specific RPC function calls. Implementing Windows Firewall RPC filtering policies provides native, low-overhead network segmentation to block malicious RPC abuse without third-party agent hooks.

## Overview

In "Synthetic Trust: Exploiting Biases at Scale," speakers Bivu and Esty Scheiner explore how advancements in AI, biometric authentication, and human subconscious biases intersect. Esty works as a security engineer at Invoca (a conversational intelligence company working at the junction of AI security and audio, primarily coding in Ruby), while Bivu works in voice authentication, fraud detection, and deepfake detection. 

They open by comparing the 1990s movie *Sneakers*—where a voice replay attack was purely Hollywood sci-fi—to today's reality, where voice recognition serves as authentication for banking and secure systems. Connecting their professional work to human psychology, the speakers examine how interpersonal biases and subconscious preferences can be analyzed, quantified, and potentially exploited.

## The Similarity Hypothesis and Hackathon Project

The speakers began exploring a long-standing concept found in literature: individuals are subconsciously attracted to and trust people who look similar to themselves. To test whether hard data could support this hypothesis, they collaborated on a hackathon project born out of "Idea Thursday" at their shared WeWork space in Boulder, Colorado:

* **Image Generation Challenges:** When generating a photo representing their team (a Nepali man and a Jewish woman working together in a basement), standard image prompts produced poor results, requiring manual Photoshop adjustments.
* **Facial Matching Application:** They built a tool that takes two photos and calculates a visual similarity match percentage. Identical twins score in the 90s, siblings typically score between 40% and 60%, and unrelated pairings can drop to single digits.
* **Data and Validation:** By scraping thousands of images from Reddit, their testing supported the hypothesis that people gravitate toward visual similarity. 

## Biases in the Workplace: Visual and Audio Features

Following their initial findings, the speakers considered broader workplace implications, such as managerial bias favoring certain groups:

* **HR Analytics Concept:** They initially conceptualized an HR tool to extract interaction features between individuals and establish a baseline of how a manager behaves on average versus how they treat specific employees.
* **Transition to Audio Analysis:** Before writing code for the HR tool, they shifted focus toward audio characteristics.
* **Linguistic and Acoustic Nuances:** Bivu highlighted how cultural and linguistic backgrounds affect vocal perception. Nepali is characterized by short-lived vowels, a relatively monotonous delivery, and a lack of strong intonation. As a result, listeners frequently misread emotional states unless the speaker intentionally exaggerates their delivery, potentially leading to misunderstandings in personal relationships and workplace evaluations (e.g., a manager incorrectly perceiving a lack of enthusiasm for a project).

## Cognitive Shortcuts and Personal Frameworks

Esty contrasted their distinct backgrounds—referencing her life dictated both by software code and the code of Kabbalah (including weekly observance of Shabbat, completely disconnecting from technology from Friday sundown to spend time with nearby family and friends). Despite broad individual differences, humans rely on mental models and cognitive shortcuts to process social interactions, forming the foundation of subconscious biases and synthetic trust dynamics.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding From Dead Data to Digestion: Extracting Windows Fibers for Your Digital Forensics Diet.

talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
A former UK intelligence researcher and WithSecure veteran explores the forensic analysis and adversarial exploitation of Windows fibers. While fibers were originally introduced in Windows 95 as cooperative multitasking primitives for high-performance server workloads, modern threat actors and command-and-control (C2) frameworks increasingly abuse them to bypass endpoint detection and response (EDR) telemetry. The talk covers the reverse engineering of fiber internals in modern Windows builds (1903+) and introduces memory forensics methodologies to extract hidden fiber execution contexts.

Key Topics:
- Windows fiber architecture and cooperative multitasking mechanics
- Structural internals across the PEB, TEB, and Thread Information Block (TIB)
- Adversarial abuse models: shellcode execution and stealthy FLS callbacks
- EDR evasion via call stack spoofing and fiber-based context switching

Technical Details:
The speaker explains that Windows fibers operate as stackful co-routines executing entirely within user mode. Unlike kernel-scheduled threads, fibers are invisible to the operating system scheduler and must be cooperatively scheduled by the application using the SwitchToFiber API. Fibers share the enclosing thread's execution context, with only one fiber active per thread at any time. The Thread Information Block (TIB)—the initial structure inside the Thread Environment Block (TEB)—maintains a pointer to the active fiber data alongside the stack limits, making fibers lightweight mini-threads without kernel context-switching overhead or traditional synchronization primitives.

Adversaries leverage the simplicity and obscurity of the Windows fiber API to achieve stealthy code execution. In a basic attack chain, a thread converts itself using ConvertThreadToFiber, allocates Read-Write-Execute (RWX) memory containing shellcode, creates a new fiber via CreateFiber targeting the payload address, and invokes SwitchToFiber. A more evasive technique abuses Fiber Local Storage (FLS): when allocating an FLS index via FlsAlloc, a developer can register a callback function that automatically executes when the fiber is deleted or the index is freed. Attackers can register malicious execution entry points in these callbacks, leaving no direct operational artifacts within the PEB, TEB, or TIB.

Fibers present substantial blind spots for contemporary EDR products. Most endpoint detection agents gather call stacks synchronously when high-risk system calls occur (such as cross-process memory access to lsass.exe). Because fiber context switches involve manual stack pointer adjustments without kernel transitions, an adversary can perform malicious staging inside one fiber, switch to an innocuous secondary fiber, and then trigger the monitored API. The resulting call stack captured by the EDR captures only the benign caller, effectively blinding behavioral inspection engines to the preceding malicious fiber execution.

Key Takeaways:
Incident responders and threat hunters must incorporate user-mode fiber inspection into memory analysis routines, as dormant fibers parked in memory hide malicious shellcode and unhooked call stacks. Security teams should monitor the invocation of fiber management APIs like ConvertThreadToFiber, CreateFiber, and FlsAlloc in untrusted processes. EDR engineering must evolve beyond single-thread call stack snapshots to reconstruct user-mode fiber state transitions during security-relevant API invocations.

talks.aiSummary:
## Overview

In the presentation *"Close Encounters of the Advanced Persistent Kind: Leveraging Rootkits for Post-Exploitation"*, speakers Ruben Boonen and Valentina Palmiotti from IBM X-Force's Adversary Services team discuss the mechanics of using vulnerable drivers and rootkits during red teaming operations. The talk explores how threat actors—spanning both state-sponsored groups and modern ransomware operators—utilize vulnerable drivers for post-exploitation tasks, and examines how attackers achieve kernel-level execution to bypass userland security controls.

## Threat Actor Landscape: Old Money vs. New Money

Boonen frames rootkit and vulnerable driver adoption across two primary categories:
* **"Old Money" (State-Sponsored APTs):** Groups such as Turla, Equation Group, and Lazarus possess high-capability toolsets and have documented histories of abusing vulnerable drivers for post-exploitation spanning more than a decade (e.g., Turla activity documented back to 2012).
* **"New Money" (Ransomware Operators):** Financially motivated actors began adopting vulnerable drivers later (around 2017 or later). While historically bringing less sophisticated tooling compared to APTs, their rapid progression highlights a narrowing gap in tradecraft.

## Driver Loading Vectors and Exploitation Windows

To deploy a rootkit via a vulnerable driver, operators must achieve initial kernel execution. The speakers highlight three main avenues:

1. **Zero-Day Vulnerabilities (0-days):** Project Zero data indicates that in-the-wild zero-day exploitation is increasing rather than leveling off. This trend is driven by researchers discovering new attack surfaces or uncovering variants of previously patched bugs when vendors fail to conduct thorough variant analysis (e.g., approximately 10 to 12 privilege escalation bugs found in Windows Common Log File System [CLFS] over a two-year span).
2. **N-Day Vulnerabilities:** When zero-days are unavailable, attackers exploit patch latency windows. Reported metrics show an average patch lag of **16 days for high and critical vulnerabilities**, and **151 days for medium and low vulnerabilities**. While corporate workstations (e.g., finance) often have rapid automated updates, business-critical systems experience substantial lag. Demonstrating this feasibility, the speakers highlighted an N-day in the Windows Ancillary Function Driver (`afd.sys`): due to insufficient user-supplied data validation allowing a semi-controlled write to a kernel address, they reverse-engineered the patch, identified the flaw, and produced a working exploit within **24 hours**—well inside the 16-day average patch window.
3. **Administrator-to-Kernel Paths:** While Microsoft does not officially recognize the administrator-to-kernel boundary as a security boundary, Boonen argues this perspective overlooks corporate realities. Home users routinely run as local administrators, and corporate network compromises in Active Directory (AD) frequently lead to privilege escalation. Once attackers attain domain administrative privileges, they can remotely access untouched target machines as admin, deploying rootkits for lateral movement and in-memory persistence on long-running servers.

## Rationale for Operating in Kernel Space

Operating within kernel space provides distinct post-exploitation advantages over userland:
* **Bypassing Userland Mitigations:** Numerous defensive mitigations exist exclusively in user mode; kernel-mode execution circumvents these constraints entirely.
* **Neutralizing Specialized Defenses:** Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions have become hyper-specialized at monitoring userland telemetry and processes, whereas kernel access enables adversaries to operate underneath these security controls.

talks.title: Does Public Disclosure of Vulnerabilities Affect Hacker Participation in Bug Bounty Programs?
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Does Public Disclosure of Vulnerabilities Affect Hacker Participation in Bug Bounty Programs?.

talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Ali Ahmad, Assistant Professor at the University of Wisconsin–Eau Claire, presents an empirical econometric study investigating how the public disclosure of patched vulnerability reports influences hacker participation and bug discovery success in bug bounty programs. Evaluating data from major crowdsourced platforms including HackerOne and Bugcrowd, the research examines whether disclosing resolved reports stimulates discovery through information sharing or suppresses it through cognitive biases. The presentation provides quantitative insights into bug bounty dynamics using a large-scale panel dataset of enterprise programs.

Key Topics:
- Information sharing vs. cognitive bias theories in bug bounty research
- Psychological concepts of cognitive fixation and functional fixedness
- Econometric panel data methodology applied to HackerOne disclosures
- Impact of public vulnerability disclosure on future bug discovery rates

Technical Details:
The research investigates two conflicting theoretical hypotheses regarding vulnerability disclosure. The positive hypothesis suggests that public disclosures provide researchers with actionable technical intelligence—revealing organizational patch velocity, responsiveness, bounty generosity, and technology stacks—thereby encouraging researcher engagement and uncovering related flaws. Conversely, the negative hypothesis posits that public disclosures impair researcher creativity by inducing cognitive fixation and functional fixedness, well-documented psychological phenomena where exposure to specific prior examples constrains creative problem-solving.

Drawing parallels to classic psychological experiments by Karl Duncker and Steven Smith, the author explains how cognitive fixation causes subjects to replicate features of provided examples unconsciously, reducing novel outcomes. In cybersecurity, hacking represents a highly creative search process. When researchers review published reports on HackerOne or Bugcrowd, they frequently succumb to functional fixedness—viewing target assets and testing methodologies only through the narrow lens of the disclosed bug. This fixation drives hunters to execute identical attack techniques against previously resolved vulnerability classes, resulting in redundant testing and diminished discovery of novel vulnerabilities.

To test these hypotheses empirically, the author scraped publicly accessible telemetry from HackerOne, constructing an econometric panel dataset spanning 368 enterprise firms. The dataset incorporated historical activity across 83,000 resolved vulnerability reports, of which approximately 8,000 reports were publicly disclosed. Utilizing econometric panel regression models to measure treatment effects over time, the study analyzed whether firms that frequently disclose patched vulnerabilities experience a higher or lower rate of subsequent valid vulnerability submissions relative to programs that maintain private reporting histories.

Key Takeaways:
Bug bounty program managers must recognize that disclosing patched vulnerability reports does not automatically boost researcher productivity and can inadvertently suppress creative testing across broad attack surfaces. Security organizations should balance transparency with targeted testing incentives, providing clear scope guidance to steer hunters away from already-hardened endpoints. Security researchers should actively guard against cognitive fixation by avoiding over-reliance on past public reports when formulating new testing hypotheses.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Accidental Discovery of a New Vulnerability in Google's OAuth Implementation.
talks.summary: Black Hat session on The Accidental Discovery of a New Vulnerability in Google's OAuth Implementation.
talks.aiSummary:
## Overview

In this presentation, Brian Smith-Sweeney introduces a case study regarding a vulnerability discovered in Google's OAuth implementation. The speaker opens with personal background, describing an innate inclination toward talking and breaking things that ultimately led to a career in security. Reflecting on past family moments and early tendencies to test boundaries, the speaker notes that security research often mirrors this mindset of questioning explicit restrictions. While noting that the vast majority of the specific technical issues discussed have since been remediated by Google, the session is framed around broader security lessons regarding implied trust, service provider relationships, and protocol interactions.

## OAuth Architecture and Implied Trust

The talk examines the fundamental mechanics and trust assumptions behind OAuth consent dialogs:
- **Authorization vs. Authentication**: OAuth is conventionally defined as an authorization framework rather than an authentication framework. It assumes the user has already authenticated and focuses on delegating access to specific resources post-authentication, representing a substantial security advancement over legacy patterns where users directly shared raw usernames and passwords with third-party applications.
- **Client Application Authentication**: While the protocol centers on delegating user permissions, an overlooked aspect of the workflow is application authentication. When a consent dialog displays an application name requesting access, the identity of that application itself must be authenticated and validated during the flow.
- **The Surface of Trust**: Many modern architectures rely heavily on implied trust within OAuth workflows—trusting how identity providers, third-party clients, protocols, and intermediate mechanisms interact with one another.

## Security Methodology and Hypothesis Testing

Smith-Sweeney connects the discovery process to his work environment at Two Sigma, characterized as a data-driven financial sciences firm:
- **Scientific Approach to Security**: At data-driven organizations, security controls are treated not as established axioms or givens, but as hypotheses that require rigorous testing and empirical validation.
- **Validating Vendor Assertions**: Security teams should not assume vendor-supplied controls operate as advertised. Instead, validating whether protocols, controls, and configurations perform as expected under adversarial or unexpected conditions is essential for discovering subtle implementation flaws.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of When a Zero Day and Access Keys Collide in the Cloud: Responding to the SugarCRM 0-Day Vulnerability.

talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Margaret Zimmerman, a cloud incident responder at Unit 42 (Palo Alto Networks), details real-world intrusions where threat actors exploited a zero-day vulnerability in SugarCRM to compromise AWS cloud environments. Following the MITRE ATT&CK framework across nine tactics, the presentation illustrates how an initial application-level remote code execution vulnerability collided with insecure cloud credential management. The speaker demonstrates how attackers successfully pivoted from the data plane of compromised virtual machines to the AWS control plane to conduct reconnaissance and compromise critical enterprise infrastructure.

Key Topics:
- SugarCRM remote code execution zero-day (CVE-2023-22952)
- Transitioning from cloud data plane (EC2) to control plane (IAM)
- Credential harvesting via unencrypted long-term AWS access keys
- Adversary cloud discovery techniques using Pacu, Scout Suite, and AWS APIs

Technical Details:
The initial access vector centered on CVE-2023-22952, a critical remote code execution flaw in SugarCRM published on January 11, 2023, with a CVSS score of 8.8. The vulnerability arose from missing input validation in SugarCRM's email templates module, allowing unauthenticated threat actors to inject arbitrary PHP code directly into the underlying host. In the investigated breaches, victim organizations hosted SugarCRM on Amazon Web Services (AWS) within Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances, exposing the underlying virtual machine environment directly to the attackers.

Upon executing code within the EC2 instances, the threat actors engaged in credential harvesting to bridge the boundary between the data plane (running virtual server instances) and the cloud control plane (AWS management APIs). Rather than being restricted to the instance, attackers extracted plaintext long-term IAM access keys starting with the prefix AKIA from the ~/.aws/credentials file located on the filesystem. These credentials granted broad identity permissions, allowing adversaries to manipulate relational database service (RDS) instances and auxiliary EC2 infrastructure across the cloud tenant.

With control plane access secured, the adversaries executed discovery commands. The initial API invocation observed in CloudTrail logs was sts:GetCallerIdentity—the functional equivalent of whoami in AWS—to retrieve the 12-digit AWS account ID, caller user ID, and Amazon Resource Name (ARN). To map tenant infrastructure, attackers leveraged living-off-the-land techniques using Pacu (an open-source AWS exploitation framework pre-installed on the host from earlier penetration testing) alongside Scout Suite, identified via distinct User-Agent strings. Adversaries targeted AWS Organizations APIs, specifically ListOrganizationalUnitsForParent, ListAccounts, and DescribeOrganization (which exposed the master root email address), and polled ce:GetCostAndUsage to determine financial spend and identify high-value operational infrastructure.

Key Takeaways:
Cloud security teams must enforce the principle of least privilege and eliminate static, long-term IAM access keys (AKIA) stored on host filesystems in favor of IAM instance profiles and temporary STS credentials. Security operations centers must actively monitor CloudTrail logs for foundational discovery calls like sts:GetCallerIdentity and unexpected queries against AWS Organizations or Cost Explorer APIs. Critical internet-facing enterprise software must be segregated from broader cloud environments using strict VPC egress filtering and segmented IAM boundaries.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of IRonMAN: InterpRetable Incident Inspector Based ON Large-Scale Language Model and Association miNing.

talks.aiSummary:
## Overview

Presented at Black Hat by researchers from CyCraft—Chung-Kuan Chen (CK), Sian-Yao Huang (Eric), and Cheng-Lin Yang (George)—the talk introduces **IRonMAN** (*InterpRetable Incident Inspector Based ON Large-Scale Language Model and Association miNing*). Operating on the frontlines of geopolitical cyber threats in Taiwan, CyCraft monitors over 200 million security events daily across government, financial, and semiconductor sectors (including tracking operations like *Chimera* targeting the semiconductor industry and long-term nation-state threat actors). Due to this massive telemetry volume, automated triage and inspection mechanisms are indispensable for security operations.

## Problem & Motivation

The presentation addresses the operational challenges facing incident response (IR) analysts:
* **Scale of Telemetry:** Analyzing hundreds of millions of daily events cannot be handled manually by human analysts alone.
* **Complexity of Command Lines:** The research specifically scopes down to process creation events and command-line arguments (CLI data). While command lines contain rich semantic intelligence critical for identifying threat actors, their flexible syntax, obfuscation, and variable formatting make them among the most complex event log artifacts to parse and analyze.
* **Black-Box Limitations of LLMs:** Modern large language models (LLMs) provide strong natural language and semantic understanding capabilities, but their black-box nature lacks explainability, which is essential for analysts needing verifiable evidence during triage and incident reasoning.

## Proposed Methodology & Systems

To address these challenges, the researchers designed a hybrid approach combining data science and cybersecurity domain knowledge:
* **CommandGPT:** A specialized language model component tailored to capture and interpret the rich semantic information embedded in complex command-line syntax.
* **IRonMAN (Interpretable Incident Inspector):** A framework combining large-scale language models with traditional association rule mining. 
* **Hybrid Synergy:** The LLM extracts semantic features and processes command nuances, while association mining complements the neural model by providing transparent, rule-grounded patterns. This integration delivers explainable and interpretable triage outputs, enabling analysts to quickly identify attack-related commands, reason about incident progression, and execute targeted response actions.

## Key Takeaways

* Relying solely on black-box machine learning models poses explainability hurdles in high-stakes incident response.
* Coupling modern LLM capabilities with traditional data-mining methods (such as association mining) bridges the gap between semantic understanding and interpretability.
* Focusing automated inspection on high-value telemetry like process creation and command-line events provides a scalable foundation that can potentially extend to other complex security event log types.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Uncovering Azure's Silent Threats: A Journey into Cloud Vulnerabilities.

talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Nitesh, a cloud and container threat researcher at Trend Micro, presents an investigation into architectural security flaws affecting managed Jupyter notebook services within Microsoft Azure Machine Learning (AML). The research analyzes how cloud service providers integrate machine learning workloads, managed virtual machines, and shared storage resources. The speaker reveals how internal automation scripts and logging misconfigurations within underlying Azure Batch nodes expose critical primary storage credentials in plaintext, allowing lateral privilege escalation across shared enterprise machine learning workspaces.

Key Topics:
- Azure Machine Learning (AML) workspace architecture and compute instances
- Shared storage integration using Azure Files and Azure Blob storage
- Underlying compute orchestration via Azure Batch nodes and tasks
- Credential exposure via start task command-line execution and standard error logging

Technical Details:
The presentation analyzes the architecture of Azure Machine Learning (AML), a managed machine learning as a service (MLaaS) platform. Within AML, users organize machine learning lifecycles through workspaces containing Jupyter notebooks, models, datasets, and pipelines. Compute instances within AML operate as managed Ubuntu virtual machines running tools such as Jupyter, VS Code, and Docker. To enable collaboration, each workspace links to default data stores connected to an Azure Storage account. An Azure Files share is mounted across all compute instances in a workspace, providing a shared filesystem for scripts and notebooks.

The architectural vulnerability centers on how Azure mounts these shared filesystems using credential-based authentication. In Azure Files, mounting a SMB share requires supplying the storage account name as the username and the storage account's primary access key as the password. The speaker investigated how the compute instances automatically configure and mount these volumes during provisioning, discovering that Microsoft's underlying infrastructure relies on Azure Batch to orchestrate virtual machine pools, nodes, jobs, and tasks.

During the node initialization phase, Azure Batch executes a defined start task located under /mnt/batch/tasks/startup. This task runs elevated bash commands via sudo to mount the Azure Files share onto the compute instance. Because the mounting script passed the storage account name and the primary access key directly as command-line parameters, Azure Batch captured and logged the entire execution command into plaintext log files: stdout.txt and stderr.txt in the startup task directory. Any standard user with local shell or notebook execution access on any compute instance in the workspace could inspect these logs to retrieve the plaintext master storage access key, instantly obtaining complete control over all data stores, blob containers, and private intellectual property stored across the tenant.

Key Takeaways:
Cloud providers and enterprise administrators must eliminate static storage account keys in automation scripts, migrating to managed identities (Azure Managed Identities) and role-based access control (RBAC) to mount cloud storage. Automated provisioning workflows must sanitize command-line arguments to prevent sensitive credentials from leaking into startup task stdout and stderr logs. Security teams monitoring MLaaS environments should audit filesystem permissions on batch startup directories and restrict multi-tenant workspace visibility to centralized storage accounts.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)
